results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included; probable disease requires four groups (or three with a teratoma) of rapid onset plus an abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: All patients had antibodies in CSF, whereas about 14% were negative in serum; CSF titres related more closely to outcome than serum titres.
results.source: Gresa-Arribas N et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:167-177

results.finding: 38% had a tumour, mostly ovarian teratoma; 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy or tumour removal; second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide after first-line failure was associated with better outcome; 81% had mRS 0-2 at 24 months.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165

results.finding: Extreme delta brush was found in 7 of 23 adults with anti-NMDAR encephalitis and was associated with a more prolonged illness.

output.summary: Published criteria and cohort data on anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: definite diagnosis rests on CSF IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies; first-line immunotherapy and tumour removal are followed by second-line agents when there is no response.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Serum anti-GluN1 positive (1:128); sodium 141 mmol/L; thyroid function, thyroid antibodies and other neuronal antibodies negative; beta-hCG negative
action_criteria.label: Obtain the reviewed serum work-up, including a cell-based IgG anti-GluN1 assay that must be interpreted with CSF rather than alone
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, toxic and infective mimics and gives the serum anti-GluN1 result, which is read with the CSF assay.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral medial temporal (right greater than left) and cingulate FLAIR hyperintensity without restricted diffusion, haemorrhage or enhancement; no structural lesion
action_criteria.label: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI to exclude HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination; a normal MRI does not exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination before LP; it is normal in most patients and does not confirm the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Lymphocytic pleocytosis (72 cells/uL), CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands and IgG index 0.91; HSV-1/2 PCR negative; CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (1:256) on cell-based assay

action_criteria.rationale: CSF anti-GluN1 IgG on a cell-based assay is the decisive test for definite disease, and HSV PCR addresses the can't-miss infectious mimic.

action_criteria.label: Obtain EEG for encephalopathic and epileptiform abnormalities, explicitly assessing for extreme delta brush
action_criteria.rationale: Seizures, dyskinesias and fluctuating consciousness need an EEG to separate seizures from movements; an abnormal EEG supports the diagnosis.

action_criteria.rationale: Women of reproductive age carry the highest teratoma risk; tumour removal is part of first-line treatment.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1-2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges); monitor capillary glucose during the steroid pulse (insulin resistance on metformin).
Arrange prompt surgical removal of the left ovarian teratoma (laparoscopic, ovary-sparing where feasible) as part of first-line treatment, with gynaecology.

Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication: increase the levetiracetam started 4 days ago (500 mg twice daily) given ongoing electrographic seizures, or add lacosamide; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.

Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for fluctuating consciousness (GCS 10-13), central hypoventilation and autonomic instability (heart rate to 145 bpm, labile blood pressure, diaphoresis), with airway assessment and cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation before cyclophosphamide.
Treat agitation and insomnia with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioural management; gynaecology for the teratoma.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.key_features: CSF HSV-1 and HSV-2 PCR negative on an LP more than 72 hours after onset; MRI medial temporal FLAIR signal without haemorrhage or restricted diffusion; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

Generalized seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability, central hypoventilation, extreme delta brush and CSF pleocytosis with oligoclonal bands are not explained by a psychiatric disorder.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-induced psychosis or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
differential.key_features: No antipsychotic or other new drug before the illness; urine drug screen negative; CK only 255 U/L; rigidity and fever accompany seizures and dyskinesias.
ANA only 1:80 with no rash, arthritis, cytopenia or other systemic feature; a maternal aunt with SLE does not change this; CSF anti-GluN1 explains the syndrome.

key_clinical_evidence: Subacute onset over about 10 days, after a viral-like prodrome, of paranoid behaviour, disorganized speech with neologisms and echolalia, generalized seizures, orofacial dyskinesias with chorea and dystonia, fluctuating consciousness (GCS 10-13) and autonomic instability with central hypoventilation: all six of the Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titre 1:256) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive 1:128 is read with the CSF.

MRI shows bilateral medial temporal (right greater than left) and cingulate FLAIR signal without restricted diffusion, haemorrhage or enhancement; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and excludes structural causes, while the negative CSF HSV PCR excludes HSV encephalitis.
EEG shows extreme delta brush with right temporal electrographic seizures; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Pelvic ultrasound shows a 2.3 cm left ovarian mature cystic teratoma: its removal is part of first-line treatment.
Earlier immunotherapy and tumour removal are associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A viral-like prodrome precedes about 70% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it does not establish viral encephalitis, which CSF PCR addresses.
red_herrings.data_point: Viral-like prodrome (myalgias, low-grade fever to 37.9 C, headache, fatigue) preceding the neuropsychiatric syndrome.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a primary viral encephalitis (HSV) or post-viral psychosis; tempts the agent to commit to empiric antiviral therapy without pursuing autoimmune workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, an abnormal EEG and CSF pleocytosis accompany the psychiatric features and require exclusion of autoimmune encephalitis before a psychiatric diagnosis is accepted.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute psychiatric presentation (paranoid ideation, insomnia, rocking and muttering) labelled an acute psychotic episode at urgent care, in a woman with no psychiatric history.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis (first-episode psychosis, brief psychotic disorder) and delays neurologic workup.

patient.history_present_illness: This 31-year-old left-handed woman of South Asian descent was brought to the emergency department by her parents after ten days of rapidly progressive neuropsychiatric decline. Approximately two and a half weeks prior to presentation, the patient developed a flu-like illness with myalgias, low-grade fever to 37.9 degrees Celsius, headache, and fatigue lasting five days. She recovered and returned to work, but within three days her mother noticed she was uncharacteristically irritable and tearful on the phone. Over the subsequent days the patient began expressing paranoid ideation, telling her parents that her coworkers were secretly monitoring her computer and conspiring to have her terminated. She stopped going to work, citing inability to concentrate and severe insomnia. Her manager contacted her parents after she failed to attend meetings for two consecutive days. When her parents visited her condominium six days before presentation, they found her apartment in disarray with uneaten food and found her sitting on the floor rocking and muttering incoherently. They brought her to an urgent care center where she was thought to have an acute psychotic episode and was referred to outpatient psychiatry. No medications were started. Over the following days at her parents' home, her confusion worsened dramatically. She developed repetitive tongue thrusting and lip pursing movements that occurred almost continuously. Four days before presentation, she had a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately two minutes with post-ictal drowsiness lasting one hour. Her parents called emergency services and she was taken to a community hospital where she received IV lorazepam 2 mg and levetiracetam 1500 mg IV loading dose. A CT head without contrast was unremarkable and she was discharged the following day with an outpatient neurology referral and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. At home, she continued to deteriorate with worsening agitation, alternating with periods of near-unresponsiveness. She had a second generalized seizure on the day of presentation. Her parents noted that she had episodes of profuse sweating and that her heart seemed to be racing. Emergency medical services found her tachycardic at 125 bpm with blood pressure of 162/100 mmHg and she was transported to this tertiary care emergency department. She was unable to provide any history. Her parents confirmed no prior psychiatric history, no recent travel, no known tick exposure, and no new medications or supplements other than the levetiracetam.

neurological_exam.additional: Pronounced orolingual dyskinesias with continuous rhythmic tongue thrusting, lip pursing, and chewing movements. Bilateral upper extremity choreiform and dystonic movements. Three episodes of sudden behavioral arrest with staring and oral automatisms lasting 10-20 seconds each observed during the 40-minute examination, highly suspicious for subclinical seizures. Autonomic instability evident with episodic tachycardia ranging from 105 to 145 bpm, diaphoresis, and blood pressure fluctuations between 130/82 and 168/98 mmHg. One brief episode of central hypoventilation observed with respiratory rate dropping to 8 breaths per minute for approximately 30 seconds before spontaneous recovery.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to perform finger-to-nose or rapid alternating movements due to encephalopathy, agitation, and involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Visual threat response present bilaterally. Facial sensation appears intact to grimace with noxious stimuli. Prominent perioral and orolingual dyskinesias with rhythmic tongue thrusting and lip pursing observed continuously. Gag reflex present. Tongue protrusion midline between episodes of involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed; patient is bed-bound due to altered mental status and requires physical restraints intermittently for safety.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but profoundly disoriented to time, place, and situation. Agitated and intermittently combative, requiring two staff members for safety. Speech is disorganized with frequent neologisms, perseveration, and tangential responses. Echolalia noted when questions are repeated. Unable to follow even one-step commands reliably. Short-term memory not testable. Glasgow Coma Scale fluctuates between 10 and 13.
neurological_exam.motor: Generalized increased tone in all four extremities with bilateral upper extremity rigidity greater than lower extremities. Strength grossly 4/5 in upper and lower extremities bilaterally when patient intermittently cooperates, but effort is unreliable. Intermittent choreiform movements of bilateral upper extremities and dystonic posturing of the right hand observed. No focal weakness identified.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 3+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses equivocal bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws symmetrically to noxious stimuli in all four extremities. Formal sensory testing not possible due to encephalopathy and agitation.
